readerTitle: When meeting in the middle fails, let the future decide
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (식당 임대 협상, B2B 소프트웨어 계약) + 실제 연구 (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999, 조건부 계약)
insight: 많은 교착 상태는 가격 다툼처럼 보이지만 실은 미래에 대한 예측이 다른 것이다. 예측 차이를 조건으로 바꾸면 둘 다 자기 예측에 걸 수 있다.
misconception: 교착 상태는 더 세게 밀거나 중간에서 반씩 양보해야만 풀린다.

sources.text: Bazerman, M. H. & Gillespie, J. J. (1999). Betting on the Future: The Virtues of Contingent Contracts. Harvard Business Review.
상가 임대의 매출 연동 임대료(percentage rent)는 쇼핑센터 임대에서 널리 쓰이는 일반 관행
식당·소프트웨어 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bazerman & Gillespie(1999) 논문의 제목, 게재 연도(HBR 1999년 9~10월호), 조건부 계약을 '예측 차이를 이용하는 방법'으로 설명한다는 내용을 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
식당 계산: 기본 임대료 $6,000 + 월 매출 $90,000 초과분의 8%. 매출 $115,000일 때 초과분 $25,000 × 8% = $2,000, 합계 $8,000(집주인 희망액과 같음). 매출 $90,000 이하이면 $6,000(점주 희망액과 같음).
소프트웨어 사례: 연 $25,000에서 시작해 6개월 차까지 주간 활성 사용자 150명 이상이면 연 $40,000 수준으로 인상. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.

cards.title: Two deals stuck in the same week
body: A restaurant owner offers $6,000 a month in rent. The landlord wants $8,000. Across town, a software founder asks $40,000 a year. The buyer offers $25,000.
Both sides tried meeting in the middle. Both sides said no. Neither deal is really about the number.

image.label: Two split scenes, each with two people pushing against one door
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눔. 왼쪽은 빈 식당 매장에서 점주와 집주인이, 오른쪽은 회의실에서 창업자와 구매 담당자가 각각 문 하나를 양쪽에서 밀고 있어 꼼짝 않는 모습. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The rent talks have stalled.
body: You're the restaurant owner. The landlord says a new office tower next door will bring crowds, so $8,000 is fair. You think the street will stay quiet for years, so $6,000 is all you can risk.
What do you propose?

options.feedback: It might close the deal. But if the street stays quiet, you pay $1,000 a month for crowds that never came, and the landlord still feels shortchanged.

options.text: Hold firm at $6,000 and say you'll look at other sites
options.feedback: Pressure can work if you truly have options. Here it just restates your prediction louder, and the landlord trusts his own prediction just as much.

options.text: Offer $6,000 base rent plus a share of sales above a set level
options.feedback: You stop arguing about who is right. If the crowds come, the landlord earns more. If they don't, you're protected. The next cards show why this works.

cards.title: The numbers were predictions in disguise.
body: Look closely at both offers. The owner's $6,000 is a bet on a quiet street. The landlord's $8,000 is a bet on a busy one.
Neither will budge, because giving ground means agreeing their own forecast is wrong. Splitting the difference doesn't settle that. It just makes both sides pay for a forecast they don't believe.
The deadlock isn't about money. It's about **what will happen next**, and nobody knows yet.

cards.title: Breaking a deadlock: change the shape of the deal
body: When positions freeze, pushing harder rarely helps. **Breaking a deadlock** means finding what the disagreement is really about, then changing how the deal is built.

Often the hidden disagreement is a prediction. Then a **contingent agreement** helps: terms that change depending on what actually happens. "If sales pass this level, rent goes up." Each side gets to bet on its own forecast.
Researchers Max Bazerman and James Gillespie argued in a 1999 Harvard Business Review article that different expectations, handled this way, can make a deal possible instead of blocking it.

image.label: A single price line splitting into two paths labeled 'if busy' and 'if quiet'
image.brief: 가운데 "Deal"에서 시작한 선이 두 갈래로 갈라짐. 위쪽 "If sales are high → higher rent", 아래쪽 "If sales are low → base rent". 두 사람이 각자 다른 갈래를 가리키며 웃는 모습.

cards.title: How the rent works out
body: If the landlord is right and sales hit $115,000, he gets his **$8,000**. If the owner is right, she pays her $6,000.

breakdown.label: Sales threshold
breakdown.detail: Monthly sales a quiet street would bring

cards.title: Same deadlock, different industry
body: Now the software deal. The buyer, a logistics company, says its drivers rarely adopt new apps, so $40,000 a year is too much. The founder is sure usage will take off.
Again, the two prices are two predictions about adoption. The fix has the same shape: tie the price to something both can watch, like weekly active users.
list: **Buying a company:** part of the price paid only if profits hit a target
cards.callout: Different industries, one move: turn the disagreement into a condition.
cards.softwareNote: Usage dashboards make this easy in software, because both sides can see the same number every week.

cards.title: Conditions only work under conditions.
body: The trigger must be clear, measurable and hard to game. A landlord who can't see real sales figures, or a buyer who quietly discourages usage to keep the price low, turns a fix into a fight.
Keep it to one or two triggers. A deal with ten conditions creates new arguments every month.
And some deadlocks aren't about predictions at all. If the other side feels disrespected or treated unfairly, a clever formula won't help. That calls for a different tool, covered next.

cards.title: Your buyer doubts their team will use it.
body: You're the software founder. The logistics company likes your product but won't pay more than $25,000 a year, because it doubts its drivers will use the app. You believe at least 150 drivers will use it weekly within six months.
What do you offer?

options.feedback: You close fast, but you've priced the deal on their pessimistic forecast. Raising it later, even if usage soars, will feel like a broken promise.

options.text: Start at $25,000, rising to $40,000 if 150 drivers use it weekly by month six
options.feedback: You both bet on your own forecast, measured on a dashboard both can see. Their risk is capped, and your upside is real if you're right.

options.text: Offer a free 30-day trial, then the full $40,000
options.feedback: A trial tests the product, but a month may be too short to show adoption. At the end, the buyer still has to believe your forecast to sign.

cards.title: When you can't agree on the future, write it into the deal.
body: Many stuck negotiations are two forecasts dressed up as two prices. Find the forecast, then make the terms depend on what actually happens.
**Try it today:** think of one stalled deal. Write down what each side believes will happen. Could one number, tracked over time, settle it?
